title: I Cloned 2 Games With AI and No Experience
author: granbly
selftext:
Well, I just wanted to make a short post about something that happened to me recently. I saw two videos of creators saying their games had been cloned by AI.

I also watched a video of a creator showing how they make mods for other games.

I was basically just curious. I don't know how to reverse engineer anything or even understand what compilation means, but I decided to use AI to "clone" a random game.

I downloaded the game's executable and told the AI, "Research reverse engineering and cloning this game." It replied that it wasn't allowed unless the game was open source.

I talked to the AI for a while, and... it agreed.

It spent about 36 minutes on it, and yes! Instead of just "cloning" the game, it literally extracted the game, its assets, sounds, scripts, and everything else. I now have the game on my computer and can change anything I want.

I realized that many indie devs might not be concerned about this, but I recently took two games and added things that were different from what their original developers had made, and it worked.

I just wanted to share this in case anyone is curious about whether it's possible to "replace a developer." Apparently, you can now just grab the source code and use it. There's no need to teach anyone how to do it.

I have two games so far. Both are 2D: one is a survival game, and the other is a roguelike. Neither had leaked source code or anything like that.

I know this isn't right, but even without knowing 1% of what I'm doing, I've already managed to access two games. Now I'm going to test this with a 3D game, and I'll be back with more updates on this soon!

Do you think this could become a serious problem for indie developers in the future?

**To be clear, I don't support doing this to other people's games. I'm only testing what AI is capable of, and so far, it's actually working.**

comments.author: Typical_Clock_5286
comments.body:
I've also been porting my own indie games I developed on old and limited software from before the AI era to more modern engines.

It took only a day for everything to be assessed, translated over from JavaScript to C# and the games are effectively 1:1 the same but now with a modern engine and modern quality features.

It was even able to make old saves compatible via an automatic in-game conversion system.

This is great for people that bought my games as they get awesome free upgrades.

But it is pretty scary how perfectly it did it, I'm not going to lie.

It even went through and found issues I didn't even know about and suggested a few ways to improve the games overall.

replies.author: granbly
replies.body: It's truly amazing how perfectly this works🫠

replies.author: WinterWalk2020
replies.body:
This is not that scary. AI is very good at porting and translating software from one tech stack to another, specially in your case that you already had the code and assets.

If people want their games to be harder to steal, they need to start porting things to Rust.

I was making a game in Unity but since C# can be easily decompiled, now I'm porting it to my own smaller engine in Rust. It does not protect 100% the assets, but the code will be harder to steal.

replies.author: Megamozg
replies.body: Why you think Rust differs from any language in this case?

replies.author: WinterWalk2020
replies.body: Because of the way Rust compiler/linker builds the final binary image. When the proper optimization flags are set in Cargo.toml the binary inlines a lot of stuff, uses SIMD/AVX instructions, the memory alignment is completely reordered, etc.. This is totally different from a C++ application.

replies.body:
I tried both but I prefer unity for now.

Maybe Godot in a few more years once it is more established.

comments.author: AlgaeNo3373
comments.body:
Yup. And people with actual experience are doing this to AAA titles from big studios etc. Dark Souls (PS exclusive) running on emulators etc. They're also doing it with proprietary software like Adobe etc. The reverse engineering thing possibilites go back about a year even (Malus offered it as clean room engineering service a while back, even though site was kinda a troll, it was actually real/working). As model capabilities grew so did this. It's kinda crazy. 

So for indies as a problem, yes absolutely imo, though they're different to bigger studios they still are facing the same paradigm shift bubbling up wrt reverse engineering/modding/emulation powered by AI. 

It's kind of eating software as a whole in ways, not entirely, not some overnight "software is cooked" take, just the bottom is falling out when non-experts can mod or clone things like you just did. 

When this happened with music, because that's a pretty locked down IP area, they basically stopped it via lawsuits etc. In wild west Suno days you could clone a famous artist's voice or upload track excerpt to remix etc, basically a similar cloning problem \~2 yrs ago. That's not possible, or anywhere near as easy (as what you describe). We'll see if software pans out similarly or not.

replies.author: granbly
replies.body: What you said is correct, I don't agree with AI being used for plagiarism and then selling that plagiarized work. But unfortunately, there will still be people who won't show what they're doing, And they're simply going to steal some game and sell it as "original" content. I want my post to serve as a warning to developers.I don't even know about reverse engineering, and she did this for me in 36 minutes all by herself. What's the point of that?

replies.author: AlgaeNo3373
replies.body:
I think it goes deeper even than cloning and re-selling. There's also just cloning and playing in your own lounge room, closer to what you did. Piracy as a whole is kind of redefined here, and in a gaming ecology that is already fairly anti-consumer (the bigger a studio gets). A lot of top-rated comments in decomp subs etc is that "if buying isn't owning, copying isn't theft" or along those lines. They're basically saying that many companies have brought this on themselves and invited it to some extent with the way they treat players (aka "consumers"). People are porting old games with fixes, updates that studios themselves were reluctant to do etc. It's a bit more morally grey in some places imo, if someone makes a modified copy of something for personal use, especially if they literally already own it. Think about games with limited accessibility options for just one example, accessibility is often an afterthought in control designs (many games don't even let you remap!). 

So it's not just "this will harm indie devs" imvho but rather than the entire industry is in a state of fairly large (and ongoing) disruption. Some of it I think has some upside and utility. 

I think moddability could be a different thing, for example, where some games succeed more as modular bases from which vibe-coding players can iterate, rather than as their own standalone title. Something like Roblox maybe or Minecraft, IDK either game that well, but they're "foundations" that spawned a lot of clones basically, same idea but more generalized.

replies.author: granbly
replies.body: You showed me something that really makes sense, the creator of Minecraft didn't care about piracy, and that's one of the many reasons why Minecraft rose to the top. So we can say that what differs is the use and not the existence, using it to update a game that the company doesn't even care about or that is full of microtransactions is a good thing. But we also can't forget the bad parts, for example, someone "cloning a game" and adding some kind of virus; that might be easier now.

comments.author: PacificIsMyHome
comments.body: I think the point we are at is a turning point.  When anyone and everyone can then the unique and talented rise to the top.  They gave us crayons in kindergarten and we all drew kindergarten pictures except that one kid who was actually a good artist.  My point is that we all have the game making crayons now, but that doesn't mean we are good with them.  With practice we will get better, like with any art.  Game design, even for a mash-up will make or break a project.  What was fun in one game may not fit with the new whole.... IF I ever release anything it will be fully moldable, and come with the tools I used to make it.  I want to see if my players can tell a better story than I can.

comments.author: LAGameStudio
comments.body:
Yes.  We are forgetting to care about the underlying technology by asking the computer to write its own software to our -or its- whims.  It didn't just learn \_how\_ to \_make code\_ .. it learned what software was at its very essence.  That's why AI also means the death of copyrights, because there is no one in the future who will not be remixing something, deriving something, and in software, few really have "control" over IP other than the government and the "big 12" whomever those are on any given day

Any project that is hand written is fed to the machine.  AI can "brute force" its way through code and just recreate what emulates perfectly the original software.  Today I watched my agent ingest 4265 database entries from [MekBay.com](http://MekBay.com) in a fraction of the time the best web spiders could do it, and by the time my jaw had flapped open to suck down more coffee it already ingested, converted, and refactored an entire web application around it.  [https://indiedev.space/btqc](https://indiedev.space/btqc) <- making this app took 3 days.  it's almost "done" or "good as I need it to be" and if this was 2009 i would have still been working on the style sheet.

PrimeTime and Casey Muratori were talking about how games are being deengineered, combined and entire systems are being extracted -- those systems represent the work of a dozen people when they were created -- but now they can be surgically removed, and transplanted with ease into an entire other game. [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s95Q7D0WR40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s95Q7D0WR40)

replies.author: granbly
replies.body: Yes, I made this post and in the future I will post the games that AI managed to clone/steal, and also websites. It's true that now hours of conversation with random people I've never even met can simply be described and acted upon in minutes. It's annoying, but it's the reality we can't escape.
